set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: What equipment does fluoroscopy require?
opts: A superconducting magnet requiring dedicated site construction beforehand and high ongoing cost
That describes magnetic resonance imaging.
A handheld transducer connected to a portable processing unit, needing neither a tilting table nor a shielded examination room
That describes ultrasound.
An x-ray unit fitted for controlled motion of the source, the imaging sensor and the patient, with a tilting table
Correct — the tube moves freely back and forth to image the patient.
A gamma camera mounted on a rotating gantry that circles the patient, with a fixed table and a detector housing that does not move
That describes single photon emission computed tomography.

set1.io: Objective g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set1.q: Why does the deck name cancer as a risk factor for all contrast material?
opts: Because the dyes provoke chronic inflammation, and chronic inflammation is carcinogenic
Inflammation is not the pathway named here for contrast-associated risk.
Because the dyes are technically radioactive, as are the imaging techniques themselves
Correct — the deck states the risk in exactly those terms.
Because the dyes are nephrotoxic, and chronic renal injury raises malignancy risk over time
Nephrotoxicity is a real risk of iodinated contrast, but it is not the reason given.
Because the dyes are retained in tissue indefinitely, and retained foreign material transforms
Indefinite tissue retention is not the mechanism the deck describes.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: What is a vasculogram?
opts: Not one specific test — any of the modalities can be used to image the vessels
Correct — x-ray, ultrasound, computed tomography and magnetic resonance all can.
A specific x-ray study in which iodine is injected directly into a peripheral vein
Angiographic studies are not confined to one modality or one route.
A specific nuclear study in which technetium is used to map perfusion to an organ
Perfusion tracers are used in nuclear medicine, but that is not what this term means.
A specific ultrasound study in which the transducer is placed within the vessel
Intravascular placement is not what the deck describes for these studies.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: Which substance is assigned a Hounsfield number of zero by convention?
opts: Fat
Fat sits below water on the scale but is not the zero reference.
Water
Correct — other tissues take a range of Hounsfield numbers according to their density.
Air
Air sits at the low, negative end of the scale.
Bone
Bone sits at the high, positive end of the scale.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: How is a conventional radiograph produced?
opts: Ionizing radiation and light strike a photosensitive surface, producing a latent image that is then processed to become visible
Correct — it requires a source, a method to record the image, and a way to process it.
High-frequency sound waves bounce off the tissue and return to a transducer, which then builds up the whole image
That describes ultrasound.
A magnetic field aligns hydrogen atoms, which emit radio waves when the field is released
That describes magnetic resonance imaging.
A gamma camera detects photons emitted by an injected radioisotope within the patient
That describes nuclear medicine imaging.

set1.io: Objective g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set1.q: What are the named indications for intravenous contrast in computed tomography?
opts: Inflammation, cancer staging, tumour delineation, vasculopathy, emboli, thrombi, stenosis and aneurysms
Correct — the vascular indications and the oncological ones are listed together.
Fracture, dislocation, foreign body, joint effusion, bone tumour, osteomyelitis and arthritis
Musculoskeletal indications of this kind are not what contrast is listed for.
Stroke, demyelination, cord compression, disc herniation, meningitis and hydrocephalus
Central nervous system tumour characterisation is listed under magnetic resonance.
Pneumonia, effusion, pneumothorax, atelectasis, emphysema and interstitial lung disease
These parenchymal lung findings are not the contrast indications named.

set1.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: What is the window in computed tomography?
opts: The range of Hounsfield numbers pre-selected for display, spread over the available grey scale
Correct — for example only those densities between −100 and +300.
The physical aperture of the gantry through which the patient passes
That is the bore rather than the window.
The interval during which the contrast sits at its peak concentration in the vessel
That is a timing concept rather than the display window.
The slice thickness selected before the scan is acquired
Slice thickness is a separate acquisition parameter.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: What does a positron emission tomography scanner use in place of an x-ray tube?
opts: A rotating fan beam, recording transmission through the patient at thousands of points
That describes computed tomography, which does transmit a beam through the patient.
A transducer, recording high-frequency sound waves reflected back from the tissue
That describes ultrasonography, which uses no ionizing radiation at all.
A varying magnetic field, recording radio waves emitted as hydrogen atoms realign
That describes magnetic resonance imaging, which is a hydrogen map.
A gamma camera, recording emissions from an injected dye in two dimensions
Correct — the radiation comes from the patient, not from the machine.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: What defines a conventional radiograph as distinct from other x-ray studies?
opts: It uses ionizing radiation together with an intravenous iodinated contrast agent
Added contrast is what a conventional radiograph lacks.
It uses no ionizing radiation at all and relies on acoustic properties instead
That describes ultrasound.
It uses a rotating fan beam and computer reconstruction into cross-sections
That describes computed tomography.
It uses ionizing radiation without any added contrast material such as barium or iodine
Correct — adding contrast makes it a different study.

set1.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: What are the five basic radiographic densities, ordered from whitest to blackest?
opts: Metal, fluid (soft tissue), calcium (bone), air, fat
Calcium is denser than fluid, and fat is lighter than air on the scale.
Metal, calcium (bone), fluid (soft tissue), fat, air
Correct — metal usually absorbs all x-rays and air absorbs the least.
Air, fat, fluid (soft tissue), calcium (bone), metal
That is the same list reversed — blackest to whitest.
Calcium, metal, fat, fluid (soft tissue), air
Metal is whiter than calcium, and fat is darker than fluid.

set1.io: Objective c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: In which patients is ultrasound named as often the first study of choice?
opts: Oncology and post-operative patients, and it is also used to stage known disease
Staging is a computed tomography and positron emission tomography role.
Female pelvis and paediatric patients, and it is also used to guide procedures
Correct — no radiation is the reason it leads in both groups.
Adult chest and geriatric patients, and it is also used to screen for fractures
Air in the lung and bone both defeat ultrasound; these are radiographic studies.
Head-injured and intoxicated patients, and it is also used to exclude a bleed
Intracranial haemorrhage is a computed tomography question in the adult skull.

set1.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: On the deck's labelled pelvic radiograph, how are bone, gas and the prosthesis described?
opts: Bone is radiopaque, gas is radiolucent, and the metal prosthesis is very opaque
Correct — one image showing three of the five densities at once.
Bone is radiolucent, gas is radiopaque, and the metal prosthesis is very lucent
Each of the three labels is inverted here.
Bone is very opaque, gas is radiopaque, and the metal prosthesis is radiolucent
Metal is the most opaque of the three, not the most lucent.
Bone is radiopaque, gas is very opaque, and the metal prosthesis is radiolucent
Gas absorbs least of anything on the film, so it is lucent.

set1.io: Objective f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set1.q: How is radiation dose defined and expressed?
opts: Ionizing energy absorbed per unit of volume, in sieverts only, where one sievert is one joule per litre
The unit of absorbed dose is the gray, and it is defined per kilogram.
Ionizing energy delivered per exposure, in millisieverts only, where one millisievert is one milliwatt
A millisievert is not a unit of power and dose is not defined per exposure.
Ionizing energy absorbed per unit of mass, in grays or milligrays, where one gray is one joule per kilogram
Correct — and equivalent dose is then expressed in sieverts or millisieverts.
Ionizing energy emitted per unit of time, in grays or milligrays, where one gray is one joule per second
Dose is absorbed energy per mass, not emitted energy per time.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: What is the stated trade-off of an open magnetic resonance scanner?
opts: Decreased quality of imaging, which is the price paid for the open configuration
Correct — it is available, but the deck flags the loss of quality.
Increased scan duration, which is the price paid for the open configuration
Time is listed as a general disadvantage, not as the open scanner's trade-off.
Increased radiation dose, which is the price paid for the open configuration
No magnetic resonance scanner emits ionizing radiation, open or closed.
Decreased soft tissue contrast only, with spatial resolution otherwise preserved
The deck says quality generally, without limiting it to soft tissue contrast.

set1.io: Objective g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set1.q: Which agent is used for magnetic resonance contrast, and what are its indications?
opts: Barium, for luminal structures anywhere from the upper oesophagus down to the rectum
Barium is an enteral agent and has no role in magnetic resonance imaging.
Gadolinium, for central nervous system tumours, metastases, soft tissue masses and arthrograms
Correct — and central nervous system tumours are typically characterised without biopsy.
Iohexol, for central nervous system tumours, metastases, soft tissue masses and arthrograms
Iohexol is the iodinated agent used in computed tomography and angiography.
Technetium-99, for bone scans, myocardial perfusion and functional brain imaging
Those are the single photon emission tomography indications, not magnetic resonance.

set1.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set1.q: What is given alongside intravenous iodinated contrast to protect the kidneys?
opts: One gram of acetylcysteine
Acetylcysteine is not mentioned in this lecture.
One dose of intravenous furosemide
Forcing diuresis is not what the deck describes for renal protection here.
One litre of normal saline
Correct — the only volume the deck specifies, and it is renal protection.
One litre of lactated Ringer's
The deck names normal saline specifically rather than a balanced solution.

set1.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set1.q: What is the stated safety record of technetium-99?
opts: Allergic reactions are rare, though documented nephrotoxicity requires pre-hydration
No nephrotoxicity has been documented for this agent.
Allergic reactions are rare, though documented hepatotoxicity requires liver monitoring
Hepatotoxicity is specifically listed as not documented.
Allergic reactions are rare, and no organ damage has previously been documented
Correct — neither nephrotoxicity nor hepatotoxicity is documented.
Allergic reactions are common, though no organ damage has previously been documented
The deck describes allergic reactions as rare rather than common.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: On a T1-weighted image, how does tissue with low water content appear?
opts: Bright, which is the reverse of the same tissue on a T2-weighted image
Correct — on T1, low water is white and high water is dark.
Dark, which is the same as that tissue would appear on a T2-weighted image
Low water content is dark on T2, and T1 reverses it rather than repeating it.
Bright, which is the same as that tissue would appear on a T2-weighted image
The two weightings invert; they do not agree on low water content.
Dark, which is the reverse of the same tissue on a T2-weighted image
This inverts both halves of the answer and is wrong on each.

set1.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set1.q: What does the deck call the most important thing to remember about ultrasound orientation?
opts: Which frequency is selected: high for superficial structures, low for deeper structures
Transducer frequency is a resolution and penetration trade-off, not orientation.
Where the indicator is: on the right of the screen in cardiac imaging, on the left for everything else
Correct — it is called crucial, because the whole image flips with it.
Where the indicator is: on the left of the screen in cardiac imaging, on the right for everything else
This reverses the convention the deck gives for the heart.
How deep the focus is set: shallow for superficial structures, deep for abdominal structures
Focal depth matters for image quality but is not the orientation rule stated.

set1.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: Which density is described as the most dense naturally occurring material?
opts: Fluid
Fluid and soft tissue share a middle density.
Fat
Fat is less dense than soft tissue.
Calcium
Correct — it absorbs most x-rays, though metal absorbs essentially all of them.
Metal
Metal is denser but is not naturally occurring in the body.

set1.io: Objective f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set1.q: How does the organ dose of neonatal abdominal computed tomography compare with the adult study?
opts: It is twice as high, twenty against ten
Correct — the smaller the patient, the higher the organ dose.
It is half as high, ten against twenty
This reverses them; the neonatal figure is the larger of the two.
It is the same, since the scanner protocol is identical
The table gives two different numbers for the two studies.
It is a tenth as high, since paediatric protocols are dose-reduced
Dose reduction is good practice, but it is not what this table shows.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: What does the colour Doppler setting add to a standard ultrasound image?
opts: Metabolic uptake and intensity, on an image otherwise showing only anatomical structure
Uptake displayed by intensity is how the positron emission studies are read.
Direction of flow and velocity, on an image otherwise made of white, grey and black
Correct — colour is the flow overlay, and blood is what it is used for.
Depth of penetration and resolution, on an image otherwise limited to superficial planes
Colour Doppler does not extend depth; poor deep visualisation remains a limitation.
Density in Hounsfield units and windowing, on an image otherwise showing five densities
Hounsfield units and windowing belong to computed tomography, not to ultrasound.

set1.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set1.q: What are the midsagittal and parasagittal planes?
opts: Midsagittal runs through the umbilicus; parasagittal sections lie above and below it
Both sagittal planes are vertical and separate right from left, not upper from lower.
Midsagittal runs across the shoulders; parasagittal sections lie anterior and posterior
That division is coronal rather than sagittal.
Midsagittal runs at the level of the heart; parasagittal sections are angled off the axis
The distinction is position relative to the midline, not level or angle.
Midsagittal runs in the body's midline; parasagittal sections lie to either side of it
Correct — the midsagittal plane is also called the median plane.

set1.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set1.q: How is a posterior-anterior chest film oriented when you look at it?
opts: As if the patient were standing behind you, with their right side on your right
The convention places the patient's right on your left, not your right.
As if you were looking at the patient's feet, with their left side on your right
That is the cross-sectional convention for tomography and magnetic resonance.
As if you were looking down from above, with their right side nearest the top
No such overhead convention is described for chest radiography.
As if the patient were standing in front of you, with their right side on your left
Correct — the same convention as facing a patient in the room.

set1.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: How does the Hounsfield table refine the five basic radiographic densities?
opts: It separates calcium from metal, which a conventional radiograph cannot tell apart
Calcium and metal are already distinct among the five basic densities.
It separates fat from air, which a conventional radiograph cannot tell apart
Fat and air are already distinguishable on a plain film.
It merges bone and soft tissue, which a conventional radiograph shows separately
The table separates tissues rather than merging them.
It separates water from soft tissue, which a conventional radiograph cannot tell apart
Correct — the deck's asterisk on “Five*” marks exactly that exception.

set1.io: Objective i — Discuss the importance of communication between the physician assistant and radiology team
set1.q: What should you do if you are unsure which modality to order?
opts: Order the study with the widest range of densities, and narrow down afterwards
Defaulting to the broadest study is not the advice the deck gives.
Order the study with the lowest radiation dose, and escalate only if it is negative
Dose matters in the diagnostic approach, but this is not the stated advice.
Order both the plain film and the cross-sectional study at the same visit
Ordering in parallel is not what the deck recommends for uncertainty.
Tell the radiologist what you are looking for, and they can guide the choice
Correct — the question you are asking is the useful thing to communicate.

set1.io: Objective c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: Which enteric pathologies is the abdominal series named as evaluating?
opts: Cholelithiasis, pancreatitis and hepatic abscess
These hepatobiliary conditions are not named for this study.
Peptic ulceration, gastritis and oesophageal stricture
Luminal mucosal disease is assessed with oral contrast rather than a plain series.
Small bowel obstruction, perforation and volvulus
Correct — the three named examples of enteric pathology.
Appendicitis, diverticulitis and inflammatory bowel disease
These are not the examples the deck gives for the plain abdominal series.

set1.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set1.q: What does the deck say about comparison films?
opts: They should be displayed only when the radiologist specifically requests them for a read
No such condition is placed on using comparison films.
They must be matched by modality but not by projection, so any old film may be paired
The pairing is projection-specific: old lateral goes beside new lateral.
They can be invaluable — old gold — and the old film is displayed adjacent to the matching new one
Correct — old posterior-anterior beside new, old lateral beside new.
They are rarely useful once a current study exists, and should be archived rather than displayed
The deck takes the opposite view of their value.

set1.io: Objective a — Identify the fundamental properties of medical imaging
set1.q: Who discovered x-rays, and what recognition followed?
opts: Godfrey Hounsfield, in Britain in 1972, awarded the Nobel Prize for Medicine in 1979
He developed the first computed tomography scanner, with Allan Cormack.
Allan Cormack, in South Africa in 1963, awarded the first Nobel Prize for Physics
He shared the 1979 Medicine prize for computed tomography.
Marie Curie, in France in 1898, awarded the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1903
Her work was on radioactivity rather than the discovery of x-rays.
Wilhelm Roentgen, in Germany in 1895, awarded the first Nobel Prize for Physics in 1901
Correct — the technique is still called roentgenography after him.

set1.io: Objective f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set1.q: In which units is radiation measured?
opts: Hertz and decibels
Those describe sound waves in ultrasound.
Millisieverts and milligrays
Correct — x-ray radiation is low compared with other radiographic modalities.
Hounsfield units and pixels
Hounsfield units measure computed tomography attenuation rather than radiation dose.
Tesla and gauss
Those measure magnetic field strength in magnetic resonance imaging.

set2.io: Objective c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set2.q: What is the decubitus position used to evaluate?
opts: Aortic calcification, because gravity displaces the overlying bowel gas out of the field
The decubitus view is not described for vascular calcification here.
Pleural effusion, because gravity lets the fluid around the lung level out and be seen
Correct — fluid in the pleural space moves when the patient is laid on their side.
Free air under the diaphragm, because gravity lets the air rise to the highest point
Free intraperitoneal air is sought on an upright abdominal series.
Bowel obstruction, because gravity separates the air from the fluid within the loops
Air-fluid levels within bowel are assessed on the abdominal series.

set2.io: Objective f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set2.q: Which disadvantages are named for conventional radiography?
opts: Operator dependence and an inability to penetrate bone or large gas-filled structures
Those are the disadvantages of ultrasound.
Long scan times and safety problems with magnetic implanted devices
Those are the disadvantages of magnetic resonance imaging.
Very high radiation dose and an inability to be made portable at all
The dose is described as relatively low and the machines can be portable.
A limited range of densities and reliance on ionizing radiation, though at relatively low dose
Correct — the dose is low compared with other radiographic modalities.

set2.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set2.q: Which term describes tissue that appears white because it absorbs more of the beam?
opts: Isodense, matching the density of the surrounding tissue
That term is not the one for a white appearance.
Attenuated, meaning the beam has been scattered away
Increased attenuation is a computed tomography term for the same idea.
Radiopaque, also called hyperdense or radiodense
Correct — less passage of x-ray photons produces the whiter appearance.
Radiolucent, also called hypodense
That describes darker tissue with greater photon passage.

set2.io: Objective f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set2.q: What is unique about radiation exposure in nuclear medicine compared with other modalities that use ionizing radiation?
opts: The exposure is delivered entirely in a single pulse rather than over a continuous scan
Exposure duration is not the distinction the deck draws for nuclear medicine.
The exposure is confined to the organ being studied rather than reaching adjacent tissue
A tracer distributes systemically; it is not confined to the target organ.
The exposure is measured in different units from those used for conventional radiography
Radiation is measured in the same units, milli Sieverts and milli Grays, throughout.
The patient can briefly become the source of radiation exposure to other people
Correct — the tracer is inside the patient, so the emission travels with them.

set2.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set2.q: Which safety issues are named for magnetic resonance imaging?
opts: Magnetic implanted devices and ferromagnetic projectiles, and it is still not recommended in pregnancy or infants
Correct — no radiation is emitted, but the magnet itself creates hazards.
Cumulative ionizing dose and radiation-sensitive organs, and it is still not recommended in pregnancy or infants
Magnetic resonance emits no ionizing radiation, so there is no dose to accumulate.
Nephrotoxicity and anaphylaxis to iodine, and it is still not recommended in renal impairment
Iodinated contrast belongs to computed tomography; this study uses gadolinium.
Operator dependence and poor penetration of bone, and it is still not recommended in obesity
Those are ultrasound limitations rather than magnetic resonance safety issues.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: How is computed tomography's place among imaging modalities described?
opts: It is the cornerstone of neuroimaging specifically
That description belongs to magnetic resonance imaging.
It is the most widely obtained imaging study performed
That description belongs to conventional radiographs.
It is the cornerstone of cross-sectional imaging
Correct — magnetic resonance imaging is described as the cornerstone of neuroimaging.
It is the safest of all the radioimaging modalities
That description belongs to ultrasound.

set2.io: Objective a — Identify the fundamental properties of medical imaging
set2.q: Which four questions frame the choice of an imaging modality?
opts: Which modality is cheapest, which is fastest, which is closest, and which the patient prefers
Cost and availability matter but are not the framing questions given.
Which modality the radiologist prefers, which is available today, which the insurer covers, and which is quickest
Those are practical constraints rather than the diagnostic framing.
Which modality gives the highest resolution, the largest field of view, the thinnest slices, and the fastest overall scan time for the patient
Technical parameters are not the framing questions given.
Which modality best rules the diagnosis in or out, is there a lower-radiation alternative, what is the risk against benefit for this patient, and is contrast needed
Correct — those are the four the lecture opens with.

set2.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set2.q: Which oral contrast agent is contraindicated when perforation is suspected, and what is used instead?
opts: Barium is contraindicated because it is toxic to extra-intestinal tissue; use gastrografin
Correct — barium outside the bowel causes alkaline burns.
Gastrografin is contraindicated because it is toxic to extra-intestinal tissue; use barium
This reverses them; gastrografin is the agent chosen when perforation is possible.
Iohexol is contraindicated because it is toxic to extra-intestinal tissue; use barium
Iohexol is the intravascular agent and is not the oral contrast in question.
Both are contraindicated because either is toxic to extra-intestinal tissue; use none
Gastrografin exists precisely so that a study can still be done.

set2.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set2.q: On the Hounsfield scale, where water is zero, which tissue sits at roughly minus forty to minus one hundred and twenty?
opts: Air, which is why it reads darker than every other tissue on the scan
Air is minus one thousand, the bottom of the scale.
Fat, which is why it reads darker than soft tissue but lighter than air
Correct — fat is negative, but nowhere near as negative as air.
Soft tissue, which is why it reads darker than fat but lighter than water
Soft tissue is positive, roughly plus twenty to plus one hundred.
Bone, which is why it reads brighter than soft tissue but darker than metal
Bone is roughly plus four hundred to plus six hundred.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What is a computed tomography image composed of, and what is each unit assigned?
opts: A series of two-dimensional projections, each one assigned its own radiodensity value as measured in millisieverts
Millisieverts measure radiation dose rather than image density.
A hydrogen map, each point assigned a relaxation time in milliseconds reflecting the local chemical environment of that tissue
That describes magnetic resonance imaging.
A matrix of thousands of tiny squares called pixels, each assigned a computed tomography number from −1000 to +1000 in Hounsfield units
Correct — water is assigned a Hounsfield number of zero by convention.
A matrix of thousands of tiny cubes called voxels, each assigned a greyscale signal intensity on a fixed scale running from zero to two hundred and fifty five
That is not how the lecture describes the image.

set2.io: Objective c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set2.q: Which tissues is magnetic resonance imaging described as the best modality for?
opts: Bone and calcified structures, essentially anything mineralised, with high spatial detail
Calcium emits no signal on magnetic resonance, which is the opposite of this claim.
Air-containing structures, essentially the lungs and sinuses, with high contrast detail
Aerated structures are a radiographic and tomographic strength, not this one.
Metabolically active tissue, essentially tumour and infection, with high functional detail
Metabolic activity is what the nuclear medicine studies are indicated for.
Soft tissue, essentially anything other than bone, with extremely high anatomical detail
Correct — the deck states it in exactly those terms.

set2.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set2.q: Which three standard planes are used in cross-sectional imaging, and how does each divide the body?
opts: Axial into upper and lower, coronal into right and left, sagittal into anterior and posterior
Coronal and sagittal are swapped; coronal separates front from back.
Axial into upper and lower, coronal into anterior and posterior, sagittal into right and left
Correct — axial is also called transverse and is the commonest of the three.
Axial into anterior and posterior, coronal into right and left, sagittal into upper and lower
Each plane here is matched to the wrong division of the body.
Axial into right and left, coronal into upper and lower, sagittal into anterior and posterior
This rotates all three assignments and is wrong on each one.

set2.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set2.q: What must be checked before giving intravenous iodinated contrast, and why?
opts: Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine, because the agent is nephrotoxic
Correct — and a litre of normal saline is given to protect the kidneys.
Liver function tests and bilirubin, because the agent is cleared hepatically
The concern named is renal rather than hepatic.
Thyroid function tests, because the iodine load can precipitate thyrotoxicosis
Thyroid effects are real clinically but are not what this deck requires checking.
Complete blood count and platelets, because the agent affects coagulation
Coagulation is not the risk the deck attaches to iodinated contrast.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: Who is credited with developing the first computed tomography scanner, and what recognition followed?
opts: Paul Lauterbur, who won the Nobel Prize for developing magnetic resonance imaging
That work was on magnetic resonance rather than computed tomography.
Sir Godfrey Hounsfield, who won the 1979 Nobel Prize in Medicine along with Allan Cormack
Correct — the unit of attenuation is named after him.
Wilhelm Roentgen, who won the first Nobel Prize for Physics in 1901
He discovered x-rays rather than computed tomography.
Allan Cormack alone, who won the 1979 Nobel Prize for Physics
He shared the 1979 Medicine prize with Hounsfield.

set2.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set2.q: Which patients are described as high risk before contrast administration?
opts: Patients with a documented anaphylactic reaction to any medication
Correct — the history that matters is anaphylaxis to anything, not to iodine alone.
Patients with a documented allergy to shellfish or to dietary iodine
The deck states there should be no cross-reactivity from shellfish.
Patients with a documented reaction to any topical antiseptic containing iodine
Topical iodine reactions are not the risk marker named.
Patients with a documented history of asthma or of seasonal allergic rhinitis
Atopy generally is not the specific high-risk marker the deck gives.

set2.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set2.q: How are radiographic projections named?
opts: In the direction the patient faces, from the side nearest the film to the side furthest away
The naming follows the beam rather than which way the patient is turned.
In the order the structures appear, from the most superficial down to the deepest tissue
Projections are not named for the order in which structures are encountered on the image.
In the position of the detector, from the cassette's near edge to its furthest corner
The detector's own geometry does not supply the name of the projection.
In the direction the beam travels, from what it strikes first to the most distal portion
Correct — so posterior-anterior means the beam enters the back and exits the front.

set2.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set2.q: On the Hounsfield scale, where water is assigned zero, what value is air given?
opts: Minus one thousand, the bottom of the scale
Correct — air absorbs least, so it takes the most negative number.
Minus one hundred and twenty, the bottom of the scale
That is the fat end of the fat range, not the value for air.
Plus one thousand, the top of the scale
Plus one thousand and above is metal, which absorbs most.
Plus four hundred, the upper middle of the scale
The four hundred to six hundred band is bone.

set2.io: Objective f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set2.q: In that same table, which listed study delivers the lowest organ dose?
opts: Screening mammography, to the breast
Three, far above any of the plain radiographic studies.
Dental radiography, to the brain
Correct — five thousandths, the smallest figure in the table.
Posterior-anterior chest radiography, to the lung
One hundredth, which is low but is twice the dental figure.
Lateral chest radiography, to the lung
Fifteen hundredths, higher than either of the two above it.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What does the deck's three-panel chest example illustrate about post-processing?
opts: The same anatomy imaged on three different modalities, compared for their relative strengths
The panels are computed tomography windows rather than different modalities.
Three consecutive time points after contrast, compared to show the pattern of enhancement
Windowing is not a timing technique.
The same acquired data re-windowed to bring out different pathology, without re-scanning the patient
Correct — that is the benefit digital imaging markedly advanced.
Three separate acquisitions at different dose settings, compared side by side for quality
Post-processing works on one acquisition; it does not require three.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: How do computed tomography angiography and magnetic resonance angiography differ in their use of dye?
opts: Computed tomography angiography injects iodine quickly; magnetic resonance angiography needs no dye
Correct — magnetic resonance angiography images the arterial walls without contrast.
Computed tomography angiography needs no dye; magnetic resonance angiography injects gadolinium quickly
This reverses them; the iodinated injection belongs to the computed tomography study.
Both inject iodine, but computed tomography angiography uses a much lower concentration
Magnetic resonance angiography is performed without contrast, so both do not inject.
Neither injects dye, because both reconstruct the vessels from the raw data afterwards
The computed tomography study does require a rapid iodinated injection.

set2.io: Objective i — Discuss the importance of communication between the physician assistant and radiology team
set2.q: Why does the deck stress giving the radiologist relevant clinical information?
opts: The radiologist repeats the study otherwise, so the history prevents duplicate imaging
Avoiding repeat imaging is described as a benefit of post-processing instead.
The radiologist has not seen the patient, so the history is what guides their read
Correct — the report is only as good as the question it is answering.
The radiologist bills separately, so the indication must be documented for the claim
Billing is not the reason the deck gives for communicating.
The radiologist selects the modality, so the history determines which scanner is booked
They can guide the choice, but the reason stated here is the quality of the read.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What determines the frequency of the radio waves a magnetic resonance scanner reads?
opts: The density of the tissue in Hounsfield units, together with the chosen window
Hounsfield units and windows belong to computed tomography.
The metabolic rate of the tissue, together with the dose of tracer given
Metabolic rate and tracer dose describe nuclear medicine studies.
The chemical environment of the hydrogen atoms, together with their location
Correct — both, which is what lets the computer build a spatial map.
The strength of the magnet in Tesla, together with the duration of the scan
Field strength changes image quality, but it is not what the deck names here.

set2.io: Objective c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set2.q: Why can magnetic resonance imaging show tissues that are surrounded by bone better than computed tomography can?
opts: Calcium emits no signal, so the bone does not obscure what sits inside it
Correct — silence from calcium is an advantage rather than a gap.
Calcium emits a strong signal, so the bone can be subtracted from the image afterwards
Calcium is silent on magnetic resonance; there is no strong signal to subtract.
Bone is windowed out during acquisition, so only the soft tissue range is displayed
Windowing is a computed tomography display technique, not a magnetic resonance one.
Bone absorbs the radio waves, so the surrounding soft tissue returns a relatively brighter signal
Bone does not absorb the radiofrequency signal in the way this describes.

set2.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set2.q: What do the terms radiolucent and hypodense describe?
opts: A whiter image, from less passage of x-ray photons through the tissue and therefore greater absorption
That describes radiopaque or hyperdense tissue.
A brighter signal on a T2-weighted magnetic resonance image of the same tissue
That terminology belongs to magnetic resonance imaging.
A region of increased uptake of an injected radioisotope on nuclear imaging
That terminology belongs to nuclear medicine.
A darker image, from greater passage of x-ray photons through the tissue and therefore less absorption
Correct — radiopaque and hyperdense describe the opposite.

set2.io: Objective f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set2.q: Which imaging devices does the deck flag as the highest-emitting currently in existence?
opts: Magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography and magnetic resonance venography
None of the magnetic resonance studies emit ionizing radiation at all.
Ultrasonography, colour Doppler ultrasonography and the hand-held bedside ultrasound units
Ultrasound uses sound waves and is called the safest of these modalities.
Computed tomography, positron emission tomography and single photon emission tomography
Correct — the deck marks this IMPORTANT, and all three use ionizing radiation.
Conventional radiography, fluoroscopy and the angiographic studies performed with x-rays
These do use ionizing radiation, but the deck calls plain films relatively low dose.

set2.io: Objective g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set2.q: What is oral contrast indicated for?
opts: Structure or disease of the intraluminal space, anywhere from the upper oesophagus to the rectum
Correct — it outlines the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract.
Structure or disease of the vascular space, anywhere from the aortic root to the digital arteries
Vascular imaging requires an intravascular injection, not an oral agent.
Structure or disease of the pleural space, anywhere from the apex to the costophrenic angle
Oral contrast does not reach the pleural space.
Structure or disease of the urinary space, anywhere from the renal pelvis to the urethra
The urinary tract is imaged with an injected or retrograde agent instead.

set2.io: Objective i — Discuss the importance of communication between the physician assistant and radiology team
set2.q: What practical ordering point does the deck make about imaging several body regions?
opts: Multiple body parts require the radiologist to countersign the request before booking
No countersignature requirement is described.
Multiple body parts must be imaged on separate days to limit cumulative radiation dose
Magnetic resonance emits no ionizing radiation, and no such rule is stated.
Multiple body parts or sections may mean multiple orders, giving brain, cervical, thoracic and lumbar spine as the example
Correct — one clinical question can require four separate requests.
Multiple body parts should be combined into one single order, so that the patient is scanned once and the radiologist reads the whole study together
The deck makes the opposite point about how these studies are requested.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What does fluoroscopy let a clinician evaluate?
opts: Direction and velocity of blood flow, viewed as colour superimposed on grey scale
Colour flow mapping is the Doppler setting on an ultrasound machine.
Motion of body parts and positioning changes of bones and joints, viewed in real time
Correct — real-time visualisation is the point of the study.
Metabolic activity in organs and tissues, viewed as intensities after tracer injection
Intensity mapping of uptake is a nuclear medicine study rather than fluoroscopy.
Water content in soft tissue and oedema, viewed on differently weighted sequences
Weighted sequences and water content belong to magnetic resonance imaging.

set2.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set2.q: Which density appears blackest on a conventional radiograph, and why?
opts: Metal, because it absorbs the most x-rays of any material
Metal usually absorbs all x-rays and appears whitest.
Calcium, because it is the densest naturally occurring material
Calcium absorbs most x-rays and appears near-white.
Fat, because it is less dense than the surrounding soft tissue
Fat is grey and somewhat darker than soft tissue, but not blackest.
Air, because it absorbs the least x-rays
Correct — greater passage of photons means a darker image.

set2.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set2.q: How does the deck summarise ultrasound's safety?
opts: Safe once screened, though implanted metallic devices must be excluded beforehand
Implanted-device screening is a magnetic resonance requirement.
Very safe, without any known major side effects at medically diagnostic levels
Correct — it is called the safest of these modalities.
Broadly safe, though a cumulative dose limit applies across repeated examinations
There is no cumulative dose, because there is no ionizing radiation.
Safe in adults, though it is avoided in pregnancy and in infants as a precaution
That caution is stated for magnetic resonance imaging, not for ultrasound.
